title: The testimony of Pareus
source_text: XXX. Ac nequis calumnietur Protestantes diversum sentire, & nos alienam ipsis affingere doctrinam, hac de re quaedam eorum testimonia velut in specimen proferemus. Nam singula persequi infinitae operae, & superfluum esset. Et res alioqui est attendenti per se satis manifesta. Igitur Paraeus scribens in Bellar. lib. 4. de Justif. cap. 10. In quaestione, inquit, est, An justificati possint legem divinam implere, quod adversarius absolute affirmat, nos de impletione imperfecta, inchoata damus, de perfecta negamus. Et postea explicans quid sit legem implere, Legem Dei implere, inquit, si absolute loquaris, est legi divinae obedientiam perfectam, sine ullo defectu, praestare, quod justificatos non posse nos docere fateor. Quibus subjungit nos docere homini justificato legem implere impossibile esse, non plane, ut nobis falso imponit Bellarminus, sed quoad legis ἀκρίβειαν, quae omnem defectum excludit, adeoque hominem in statu gratiae posse legem implere inchoate, hoc est, novam obedientiam legis, secundum omnia ejus praecepta inchoare: non posse vero implere absolute sine omni peccato.
pass_a_gloss: XXX. And lest anyone slander that the Protestants think differently, & that we foist on them a doctrine foreign to them, we will bring forward some of their testimonies on this matter as a specimen. For to pursue them one by one would be a work of infinite labour, & superfluous. And the matter is otherwise manifest enough of itself to one who pays attention. Accordingly Pareus writing on Bellar. book 4. de Justif. chap. 10. In question, he says, is, Whether the justified can fulfil the divine law, which the adversary affirms absolutely, we grant concerning an imperfect, begun fulfilment, we deny concerning the perfect. And afterwards explaining what it is to fulfil the law, To fulfil the law of God, he says, if you speak absolutely, is to render to the divine law a perfect obedience, without any defect, which I confess we teach the justified cannot do. To which he adds that we teach that to fulfil the law is impossible for the justified man, not plainly, as Bellarmine falsely imputes to us, but as to the ἀκρίβειαν (exactness) of the law, which excludes every defect, & accordingly that man in the state of grace can fulfil the law inchoately, that is, begin the new obedience of the law, according to all its precepts: but cannot fulfil it absolutely without any sin.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXX. So that no one can falsely allege that Protestants think otherwise, or that we are pinning on them a doctrine not their own, we will cite a few of their statements on the matter as a sample. To go through them all would be endless labour, and needless; besides, the matter is plain enough to anyone who pays attention.

Pareus, then, writing on Bellarmine's De justificatione, book 4, chapter 10, says: 'The question is whether the justified can fulfil the divine law. Our opponent affirms it absolutely; we grant it of an imperfect, begun fulfilment and deny it of a perfect one.' Later, explaining what fulfilling the law means, he says: 'To fulfil God's law, speaking absolutely, is to give the divine law a perfect obedience without any defect, and I confess we teach that the justified cannot do this.'

He goes on to say that we teach fulfilling the law is impossible for a justified person, not outright, as Bellarmine falsely charges us, but with respect to the law's exactness (ἀκρίβεια), which rules out every defect. A person in the state of grace can therefore fulfil the law in a begun way, that is, begin the new obedience of the law according to all its precepts, but cannot fulfil it absolutely, without any sin.
